name: Baking Ingredients
summary: What flour, sugar, fat, eggs, leaveners and salt each do in a bake, so you know what changes when you swap one.

sections.heading: Flour
blocks: Flour gives a bake its structure. Mixed with water, two of its proteins form **gluten**, a stretchy network that traps gas. More protein means more gluten: chewier bread, but tougher cakes.

rows: Almost everything: cookies, quick breads, pancakes, pie crust, everyday bread.
High, but the bran cuts the gluten
Nuttier, denser bakes; it drinks more liquid, so start by swapping a quarter of the white flour.
A very finely milled Italian flour, used for Neapolitan-style pizza and pasta.

blocks: The more you mix flour with liquid, the more gluten develops. That's what you want in bread dough and what you avoid in muffins and pancakes; see [mixing methods](guide:mixing-methods).

sections.heading: Sugar
blocks: Sugar does far more than sweeten. It holds on to moisture (softer, longer-keeping bakes), browns the crust, makes cookies spread and keeps cakes tender. Cutting the sugar in a recipe by more than about a quarter changes the texture, not just the taste.

items: **Brown:** granulated sugar with molasses. It's moister and slightly acidic, so it makes cookies chewier and helps baking soda work.
**Powdered (confectioners'):** finely ground with a little cornstarch, for icings and some shortbreads. Not a one-for-one swap for granulated.

sections.heading: Fat
blocks: Fat makes bakes tender by coating flour so less gluten forms, and it carries flavor.

items: **Butter** has the best flavor. It's only about 80% fat; the rest is mostly water, which turns to steam and helps flaky doughs lift.
**Oil** is pure fat and stays liquid, so it makes moist, soft cakes and quick breads, but nothing flaky or creamed.
**Shortening** is pure fat that stays solid at room temperature: tender, flaky crusts with little flavor.

blocks: Butter's temperature changes the result as much as the amount:

rows: Pie crust, biscuits, scones: pieces of it make flaky layers.
About 65°F (18°C). A finger presses a dent without sinking in; it's cool, not shiny or greasy.
Creaming with sugar for cookies and cakes.
Brownies, many quick breads, pancakes: denser and chewier.

blocks.text: The recipes here use unsalted butter so the salt is under your control. Salted butter works; use a little less salt (see [substitutions](guide:baking-substitutions)).

sections.heading: Eggs
blocks: Eggs bind, add structure as they set, help things rise (especially beaten), and add richness from the yolk. Recipes mean **large** eggs unless they say otherwise.

blocks.text: Room-temperature eggs mix in more evenly and don't firm up softened butter. Forgot to take them out? Leave them in a bowl of warm tap water for 5–10 minutes.

sections.heading: Baking soda and baking powder
blocks: Both make bubbles of carbon dioxide that lift a batter, but they aren't interchangeable.

rows: An acid in the recipe: buttermilk, yogurt, sour cream, brown sugar, honey, natural cocoa, lemon juice.
About 3–4 times stronger than baking powder. It starts working as soon as it's wet, so bake soon after mixing. It also helps browning.
Nothing: it's baking soda with a dry acid already mixed in.
Most sold in the US is double-acting: some lift when it's wet, more in the oven's heat.

blocks: Many recipes use both: soda to balance an acid ingredient, powder for the rest of the lift. Too much of either tastes bitter or soapy and can make a bake rise fast and then sink.

blocks.text: Both go flat with age. To test baking powder, stir ½ tsp into hot water: it should fizz right away. For baking soda, add a few drops of vinegar to ¼ tsp.

blocks: Dutch-process cocoa has been treated to remove its acidity, so it doesn't activate baking soda the way natural cocoa does. Recipes written for one aren't always right with the other.
Yeast is a different kind of leavener, living rather than chemical; see [yeast dough](guide:yeast-dough).

sections.heading: Salt
blocks: A little salt makes sweet things taste more like themselves, and in bread it strengthens gluten and keeps the yeast in check.

Salts differ a lot by volume: a teaspoon of table salt is about twice as salty as a teaspoon of Diamond Crystal kosher salt, because kosher flakes are bigger and pack loosely. In these recipes plain "salt" means table or fine sea salt; see the [spoon weights](guide:measuring-for-baking#spoons).

sections.heading: Milk, buttermilk and yogurt
blocks: Milk adds moisture, richness and browning. Buttermilk, yogurt and sour cream do the same and add acid, which tenderizes and feeds baking soda; that's why the [pancakes](recipe:buttermilk-pancakes) use both buttermilk and soda. No buttermilk? See [substitutions](guide:baking-substitutions).

rows: Paler, drier, less tender; cookies spread less.
Drier, denser, more cakey; cookies spread less.
Denser and chewier; cookies spread more.
Moister and softer, less buttery flavor, nothing flaky.
Chewier and taller; tougher in cakes.
